Sensuous

/SEN-shoo-uhs/ - the stress falls on SEN · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sensuous means richly appealing to the senses, especially in art, music, or nature.

Readers forgive the plot because the book's prose is so sensuous: you can smell the cedar smoke and feel the fog settle.

Worked Example

The perfume house's catalog is famously sensuous writing: amber described as lamplight you can wear, vetiver as rain on a gravel road, each page more atmosphere than chemistry.

Sensuous praises richness offered to the senses, especially by art, music, writing, or nature. It was coined to stay respectable — poets wanted 'appealing to the senses' without sensual's bodily wink — and the split held: a sensuous cello line, a sensual feast.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lush: Lush means richly abundant — thick greenery, deep pile, layered harmonies; it counts how much is there. Sensuous is about where richness lands: on the senses, especially through art, music, prose, or landscape. An overgrown garden is lush; the poem that makes you smell it is sensuous.

evocative: Evocative art works by association: it stirs memories and feelings of something else — a song that brings back one summer. Sensuous art works on the senses directly, rich in texture, color, and sound in itself. Evocative points you elsewhere; sensuous holds you in the present moment.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

stark: bare and unsoftened

clinical: coolly efficient, with all feeling drained out

Where it sits · how completely the richness floods you — vivid → sensuous → ravishing

vivid vs. sensuous: Vivid stops short of sensuous — it sharpens a single image, while sensuous richness fills every sense at once.

ravishing vs. sensuous: Ravishing goes further than sensuous — sensuous beauty invites you to linger, while ravishing beauty overwhelms you outright.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sens-

Root — sens-: to feel, to perceive (Latin sentire)

Suffix — -uous

Suffix — -uous: full of, given to

Put it together

Put it together: Sens- (Latin sentire, 'to feel') + -uous ('full of') = full of the senses. The poet John Milton is often credited with coining sensuous in the 1640s precisely because sensual had grown a smirk — he wanted a clean word for art that feeds the eye and ear. The pair still divide the labor exactly there.

Use the root in a new word: sensory

Use the root in a new word: sensory: The museum's new sensory room lets visitors handle raw wool, crushed lavender, and cold river stones.

Word Choice

literary / appreciative

Sensuous is the reviewer's word for richness to the senses in art, music, prose, or landscape. Sensual (also in this unit) keeps the body and its appetites. The border blurs in casual speech, but careful writers hold it: sensuous brushwork, sensual comfort — and on the SAT, the painting gets sensuous.
